paras: The attempted lynching of Joseph Stout was a threatened mob hanging in Montgomery County, Indiana, on the night of November 25, 1882, when mobs gathered at Colfax and Darlington to seize Stout as officers took him by train to the Crawfordsville jail. Stout had been arrested in Indianapolis that day, accused of murdering and robbing a Darlington grocer, Taylor Dunbar. The officers left the train early and drove to Crawfordsville, where Stout was jailed unharmed, and wire reports carried the story under headlines about his narrow escape.

According to an Indianapolis dispatch of November 26, Dunbar's body was found in a cornfield near Darlington on the preceding Friday, with wounds to the head and upper body. He had left home with Stout, a young man of the town, and when Stout could not be found suspicion fell on him. Deputy Constable Marshall of Darlington, described as a friend of Dunbar, arrested Stout in an Indianapolis variety theatre, where he was said to have blood on his shirt and a pawn ticket for Dunbar's watch. The dispatch said Stout confessed on the way back to clubbing and shooting Dunbar in a wood about four miles from town and taking four dollars and a silver watch.

"Intense excitement" was reported in Darlington, and the same dispatch said it was feared the prisoner would be lynched. That night, as Stout was being taken to Crawfordsville, mobs were organized at Colfax and Darlington, towns on the rail route, "for the purpose of hanging him." Warned of this, the officers in charge left the train at Thorntown and drove on by wagon.

They were headed off at one or two places along the way but, by rapid driving, reached the Crawfordsville jail with Stout unharmed. The papers give no size for the mobs and name none of their members, and they do not state the race of Stout, Dunbar or the crowds.
The dispatch closed with the fear that a further effort would be made to take Stout from the jail and hang him. No report of an attack on the jail, an indictment or a trial was found in the coverage.

The story reached papers from New York and Wheeling to Savannah and Lancaster on November 27, all from the same Indianapolis dispatches. Headlines put the murder first, as in the Wheeling Register's "COLD BLOODED MURDER," while the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer and the Savannah Morning News framed the episode as a murderer who "narrowly" or "barely" escaped lynching. The wire text treated Stout's guilt as settled, calling him "worthless" and "of unsavory reputation" while describing Dunbar as a man of family who "stood well in the community."

Later items repeated this contrast: the Bismarck Tribune called Stout "a worthless vagabond" and wagered "ten to one" that he would be lynched, without criticism of the mob. The Ottawa Free Trader's account of December 2 retold the murder and confession without mentioning the mobs. No Black-press coverage of the case was found.
